author: Todd Feldman
title: Recession And Treasury Yield Inversion
text:
The Treasury yield curve has inverted between the fifth and third year maturities. The purpose of this article is to determine what the inversion means for the US economy.
I downloaded data from the Federal Reserve's website. Daily data starts from 1962 onward. Below is a figure of only negative spreads from 1962 onward.
The spread between the five and three year Treasury yield has turned negative before every US recession from 1962. There were not any false positives except one may argue in the mid 1960s. The spread did turn negative in 1964 and stayed at zero or negative from 1964 all the way up until 1969 when a mild recession hit. Below is a table of the periods where the spread turned negative and the corresponding US recessions. The recession timeline commentary was taken from Wikipedia. The negative yield spread period is defined as the year when the spread turned negative to the year when it turned back to positive. I also included the 10-1 year Treasury yield spread.
Table: 5-3 year Treasury Yield Inversion and US Recessions
5-3 Year Negative Spread Period 10-1 Year Negative Spread Period Recession Period Recession Duration Description 1964-1970 1965-1970 Dec 1969-Nov 1970 11 months The relatively mild 1969 recession followed a lengthy expansion. At the end of the expansion, inflation was rising, possibly a result of increased deficits. This relatively mild recession coincided with an attempt to start closing the budget deficits of the Vietnam War (fiscal tightening) and the Federal Reserve raising interest rates (monetary tightening). 1973-1974 1973-1974 Nov 1973-Mar 1975 4 months The 1973 oil crisis, a quadrupling of oil prices by OPEC, coupled with the 1973–1974 stock market crash led to a stagflation recession in the United States. 1978-1982 1978-1982 Jan 1980-July 1980 6 months The NBER considers a very short recession to have occurred in 1980, followed by a short period of growth and then a deep recession. 1978-1982 1978-1982 July 1981-Nov 1982 10 months The Iranian Revolution sharply increased the price of oil around the world in 1979, causing the 1979 energy crisis. This was caused by the new regime in power in Iran, which exported oil at inconsistent intervals and at a lower volume, forcing prices up. Tight monetary policy in the United States to control inflation led to another recession. 1988-1990 1989-1990 July 1990-Mar 1991 8 months After the lengthy peacetime expansion of the 1980s, inflation began to increase and the Federal Reserve responded by raising interest rates from 1986 to 1989. This weakened but did not stop growth, but some combination of the subsequent 1990 oil price shock , the debt accumulation of the 1980s, and growing consumer pessimism combined with the weakened economy to produce a brief recession. 1998-2000 1998-1990 Mar 2001-Nov 2001 8 months The collapse of tech bubble, Enron, and terrorist shocks. 2005-2008 2006-2008 Dec 2007-June 2009 1 year The subprime mortgage crisis led to the collapse of the United States housing bubble. The amount of time from inversion to recession varies greatly. It can take one year to five years. The 10-1 year yield almost always inverted in the same time span as when the 5-3 year yield inverted. The one example when there was a larger time lag between the two spreads inverting was in 1964 and 1965. The 5-3 year spread inverted at the end of 1964 and the 10-1 year spread inverted at the end of 1965. There was a one year time lag between the two both inverted at the same time.
My expectation is that the 10-1 year won't invert for some time. If this is the case then the current economic trajectory may play out in a similar to way as in 1969-1970 recession. The mid to late 60s Treasury yield curve was inverted the majority of the time. Then the recession that followed was relatively mild. If this is the case then I see no reason to stay out or sell investments in the US stock market if solely looking at the Treasury yield curve. In my previous article , I suggested we are still in the beginning of a long-term bull cycle. Therefore, it would make sense that a recession won't happen for several years and the reason will be mild. Therefore, I recommend the US stock market investing in ETFs such as SPY or large capitalization stocks such as AAPL and AMZN.
